concepts.label: Agriculture in India
concepts.cardText: India is an agriculturally important country. Two-thirds of its population is engaged in agricultural activities. Agriculture is a primary activity, which produces most of the food that we consume. Besides food grains, it also produces raw material for various industries, and some agricultural products like tea, coffee and spices are exported.

concepts.label: Farming Systems in India
concepts.cardText: Agriculture is an age-old economic activity in our country. Over the years cultivation methods have changed significantly depending upon the characteristics of the physical environment, technological know-how and socio-cultural practices. Farming varies from subsistence to commercial type.

concepts.label: Primitive Subsistence Farming
concepts.cardText: Primitive subsistence agriculture is practised on small patches of land with primitive tools like hoe, dao and digging sticks, and family or community labour. It depends upon monsoon and the natural fertility of the soil. It is 'slash and burn' agriculture: farmers clear a patch, grow food crops, and when the soil fertility decreases they shift to a fresh patch, which lets nature replenish the soil. Productivity is low because no fertilisers or modern inputs are used. It is called jhumming in the north-eastern states.

concepts.label: Intensive Subsistence Farming
concepts.cardText: Intensive subsistence farming is practised in areas of high population pressure on land. It is labour-intensive farming, where high doses of biochemical inputs and irrigation are used for obtaining higher production. The right of inheritance divides land among successive generations and has made land-holding size uneconomical, yet farmers continue to take maximum output from the limited land in the absence of an alternative source of livelihood, so there is enormous pressure on agricultural land.

concepts.label: Commercial Farming
concepts.cardText: The main characteristic of commercial farming is the use of higher doses of modern inputs, such as high yielding variety (HYV) seeds, chemical fertilisers, insecticides and pesticides, in order to obtain higher productivity. The degree of commercialisation of agriculture varies from one region to another. For example, rice is a commercial crop in Haryana and Punjab, but in Odisha it is a subsistence crop.

concepts.label: Plantation Agriculture
concepts.cardText: Plantation is also a type of commercial farming. A single crop is grown on a large area. The plantation has an interface of agriculture and industry. Plantations cover large tracts of land, using capital intensive inputs, with the help of migrant labourers, and all the produce is used as raw material in the respective industries. Tea, coffee, rubber, sugarcane and banana are important plantation crops. Since production is mainly for the market, a well-developed network of transport and communication connecting the plantation areas, processing industries and markets plays an important role.

concepts.label: Cropping Seasons: Rabi, Kharif and Zaid
concepts.cardText: India has three cropping seasons: rabi, kharif and zaid. Rabi crops are sown in winter from October to December and harvested in summer from April to June; wheat, barley, peas, gram and mustard are important rabi crops, helped by winter precipitation from western temperate cyclones. Kharif crops are grown with the onset of monsoon and harvested in September-October; paddy, maize, jowar, bajra, tur, moong, urad, cotton, jute, groundnut and soyabean are important. In between, a short summer season called zaid produces watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, vegetables and fodder crops.

concepts.label: Rice
concepts.cardText: Rice is the staple food crop of a majority of the people in India. India is the second largest producer of rice in the world after China. It is a kharif crop that requires high temperature (above 25 degrees C), high humidity and annual rainfall above 100 cm; where rainfall is less it grows with the help of irrigation. Rice is grown in the plains of north and north-eastern India, coastal areas and deltaic regions, and a dense network of canal irrigation and tubewells has made it possible to grow it in Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh and parts of Rajasthan.

concepts.label: Wheat
concepts.cardText: Wheat is the second most important cereal crop and the main food crop in the north and north-western part of the country. This rabi crop requires a cool growing season and bright sunshine at the time of ripening, and 50 to 75 cm of annual rainfall evenly distributed over the growing season. There are two important wheat-growing zones: the Ganga-Satluj plains in the north-west and the black soil region of the Deccan.

concepts.label: Millets
concepts.cardText: Jowar, bajra and ragi are the important millets grown in India. Though known as coarse grains, they have very high nutritional value; ragi is very rich in iron, calcium, other micro nutrients and roughage. Jowar is the third most important food crop with respect to area and production, a rain-fed crop mostly grown in moist areas which hardly needs irrigation. Bajra grows well on sandy soils and shallow black soil. Ragi is a crop of dry regions and grows well on red, black, sandy, loamy and shallow black soils.

concepts.label: Pulses
concepts.cardText: India is the largest producer as well as the consumer of pulses in the world. Pulses are the major source of protein in a vegetarian diet; tur (arhar), urad, moong, masur, peas and gram are the major ones. Pulses need less moisture and survive even in dry conditions. Being leguminous crops, all of them except arhar help restore soil fertility by fixing nitrogen from the air, so they are mostly grown in rotation with other crops.

concepts.label: Sugarcane
concepts.cardText: Sugarcane is a tropical as well as a subtropical crop. It grows well in hot and humid climate with a temperature of 21 degrees C to 27 degrees C and an annual rainfall between 75 cm and 100 cm; irrigation is required in regions of low rainfall. It can be grown on a variety of soils and needs manual labour from sowing to harvesting. India is the second largest producer of sugarcane after Brazil. It is the main source of sugar, gur (jaggery), khandsari and molasses.

concepts.label: Oil Seeds
concepts.cardText: In 2020 India was the second largest producer of groundnut in the world after China. Different oil seeds are grown covering approximately 12 per cent of the total cropped area. The main oil seeds are groundnut, mustard, coconut, sesamum (til), soyabean, castor seeds, cotton seeds, linseed and sunflower. Most are edible and used as cooking mediums, but some are raw material for soap, cosmetics and ointments. Groundnut is a kharif crop and accounts for about half of the major oilseeds; linseed and mustard are rabi crops.

concepts.label: Tea
concepts.cardText: Tea cultivation is an example of plantation agriculture. It is an important beverage crop introduced in India initially by the British, and today most tea plantations are owned by Indians. The tea plant grows well in tropical and sub-tropical climates with deep, fertile, well-drained soil rich in humus and organic matter. Tea bushes require a warm and moist frost-free climate all through the year, and frequent showers evenly distributed over the year ensure continuous growth of tender leaves. Tea is labour-intensive and requires abundant, cheap and skilled labour, and it is processed within the tea garden to restore its freshness. Major tea-producing states are Assam, the hills of Darjeeling and Jalpaiguri in West Bengal, Tamil Nadu and Kerala.

concepts.label: Horticulture Crops

concepts.label: Need for Institutional Reforms in Agriculture
concepts.cardText: Sustained use of land without compatible techno-institutional changes has hindered the pace of agricultural development. Most farmers still depend on the monsoon and natural fertility, which is a serious challenge for a growing population. Agriculture, which provides livelihood for more than 60 per cent of the population, needs serious technical and institutional reforms. After Independence, collectivisation, consolidation of holdings, cooperation and abolition of zamindari were given priority. Land reform was the main focus of the First Five Year Plan; the right of inheritance had already fragmented holdings, so consolidation was needed, but the laws were enacted while implementation was lacking or lukewarm.

concepts.label: Green Revolution and White Revolution
concepts.cardText: The Government of India embarked upon agricultural reforms to improve Indian agriculture in the 1960s and 1970s. The Green Revolution, based on package technology, and the White Revolution (Operation Flood) were some of the strategies initiated to improve the lot of Indian agriculture. But this too led to the concentration of development in a few selected areas. Therefore, in the 1980s and 1990s a comprehensive land development programme was initiated, which included both institutional and technical reforms.

concepts.label: Support Measures for Farmers
concepts.cardText: The land development programme included provision for crop insurance against drought, flood, cyclone, fire and disease, and the establishment of Grameen banks, cooperative societies and banks to give farmers loans at lower rates of interest. The Kisan Credit Card (KCC) and the Personal Accident Insurance Scheme (PAIS) were introduced for farmers' benefit, along with special weather bulletins and agricultural programmes on radio and television. The government also announces minimum support price, remunerative and procurement prices for important crops to check the exploitation of farmers by speculators and middlemen.

concepts.label: Bhoodan and Gramdan
concepts.cardText: Mahatma Gandhi declared Vinoba Bhave his spiritual heir. After Gandhiji's martyrdom, Vinoba Bhave undertook padyatra across almost the entire country to spread Gandhiji's message. At Pochampally in Telangana, poor landless villagers demanded land. Shri Ram Chandra Reddy stood up and offered 80 acres to be distributed among 80 landless villagers; this act was known as Bhoodan. Some zamindars, owners of many villages, offered to distribute villages among the landless, which was known as Gramdan, and many land-owners gave part of their land out of fear of the land ceiling act. The movement is also known as the Blood-less Revolution.
